references.title: Kim Daehyeon — Frontend Developer Resume Portfolio
references.format: Public one-page, wide-format PDF resume portfolio
references.why_relevant: A Korean three-year frontend developer compresses profile, career history, projects, awards, and activities into one continuous page. Each major engagement repeats Challenge and Solutions sections, names technologies, and reports outcomes such as FCP, LCP, bundle-size, and funnel-drop improvements. It is a strong reference for evidence density and weak as a literal A4 layout model.
reusable_patterns: Use a short positioning statement that connects engineering values to team outcomes.
Repeat a Challenge, Solution, and measured result structure for each substantial engagement.
Name the technical intervention beside the observed performance or product effect.
Include contribution evidence outside paid employment, such as a merged open-source component and its tests.
cautions: The 995-by-956-point single-page canvas is not A4 and produces very small text when printed.
The large number of bullets and projects makes ownership boundaries and the strongest two achievements harder to find.

references.title: Lee Hanbyeol — Frontend Developer Resume
references.format: Public six-page A4 PDF resume portfolio
references.why_relevant: This Korean junior frontend example uses true A4 pages and shows how an early-career candidate combines a profile, skills, short employment history, projects, education, training, open-source contributions, and a longer self-introduction. Project bullets include specific user-test findings and a before-and-after interaction time of 1.2 seconds to 0.01 seconds, showing how junior work can still supply evidence.
reusable_patterns: Open with a one-sentence professional promise and three proof-oriented profile bullets.
Use a stable left label column and a wider content column for career, projects, education, and activities.
Link project claims to a portfolio, repository, blog entry, or merged contribution where available.
Include team role, duration, product context, technical action, and observable result even for bootcamp projects.
cautions: The decorative mint texture and portrait consume substantial first-page space and may reproduce unevenly on office printers.
Six pages are defensible for an early-career combined resume and portfolio, but the later prose should be shortened when a separate cover letter is submitted.

references.title: How to Write a Service-Planning Portfolio, with Sample PDF
references.format: First-person Korean hiring retrospective with a linked 10-page, 16:9 sample PDF
references.access_status: Public article and downloadable sample; no sign-in required
references.why_relevant: The author describes selecting about five HCI and service-planning projects, reducing the set to about three when a company imposed a length limit, and later critiques the sample for small type and excessive text. The sample itself establishes each project with a Problem, Solution, Result overview plus role, work type, and dates before expanding into research and design evidence.
reusable_patterns: Maintain a broader master portfolio, then select roughly three role-relevant projects for constrained applications.
Begin each project with the conclusion: claim, role, relevance to the target job, and result.
Use a Problem, Solution, and Result overview before detailed research or delivery artifacts.
Increase image size, use descriptive subheadings, underline or call out the key point, and reduce specialist language.
Tailor the cover and accent color to the company while keeping the underlying information architecture stable.
cautions: The sample is a 16:9 slide PDF rather than A4 and contains text too small for comfortable review.
The author explicitly advises spending less effort on decoration and more on making the content visible and quickly understandable.

references.title: pxd UX/UI Designer Hiring Requirements
references.format: First-party Korean UX consultancy hiring notice
references.why_relevant: A first-party Korean employer specifies a PDF portfolio under 50 MB, asks applicants to place their most confident project first, and requires contribution and work performed to be described. Although published in 2018, it gives direct evidence for submission hygiene and reviewer priorities in the local UX market.
reusable_patterns: Lead with the strongest and most role-relevant project instead of chronological order.
State individual contribution and the work actually performed, not only the team outcome.
Deliver a self-contained PDF with a predictable professional filename.
Keep the file comfortably below the stated upload or email limit and avoid archive files.
cautions: The notice is historical, so applicants must re-check the current employer's format and size limits.
A file-size ceiling is a submission constraint, not permission to fill the document with unnecessary pages.

references.title: Wanted Developer Report
references.why_relevant: Wanted reports survey and platform data from the Korean developer hiring market. Among respondents with interviewer experience, communication ability was selected by 77.6%, project experience by 75.0%, growth potential by 61.2%, and portfolio by 43.1%. This supports treating the portfolio as evidence for communication, projects, and learning rather than as a standalone gallery.
reusable_patterns: Make communication visible through concise explanations of decisions, collaboration, and tradeoffs.
Give project experience more space than generic skill inventories or personal-branding material.
Show growth potential with learning loops, changed judgment, and evidence of applying feedback.
Use one data point or chart per page with a plain-language takeaway, following the report's editorial hierarchy.
cautions: The survey reflects its collection period and should guide priorities rather than be treated as a current universal ranking.
The report evaluates hiring factors broadly; it is not a prescriptive portfolio template.

references.title: How to Build a Notion Portfolio
references.access_status: Public article; availability may depend on Wanted's page delivery
references.why_relevant: Wanted advises candidates to explain the method used to create a result, not merely name a large project or client. It recommends a short opening identity, career evidence, role-relevant personal channels and projects, and—for experienced managers—a failure case that explains the cause, learning, and subsequent behavior change.
reusable_patterns: Describe how the result was achieved, including the candidate's method and judgment.
Place a short professional identity and career sequence before optional skills and personal channels.
Include only personal projects, writing, or videos that demonstrate role expertise.
For experienced candidates, use one failure case structured as cause, action, learning, and changed practice.
cautions: Notion-specific elements such as emoji, toggles, and nested pages need a flattened PDF treatment.
Failure stories should show accountability and a verified change in practice, not performative vulnerability.

references.title: How Should a UX/UI Designer Portfolio Work in the AI Era?
references.format: Korean technology-media article on portfolio format and interaction
references.why_relevant: This contemporary Korean article recommends using PDF and web formats together: first establish the full layout and content in PDF, then adapt it into a long-scroll web experience. It clarifies a practical local-market split in which the PDF provides stable review and the website supplies interaction, motion, and expandable evidence.
reusable_patterns: Treat the PDF as the canonical, stable review artifact and the website as an optional evidence layer.
Keep project titles, section order, claims, and visual identity consistent across PDF and web.
Use the PDF to summarize interactive behavior with static frames, then link to a live prototype or web case study.
Design a vertical narrative that can map cleanly to both paginated A4 and a one-scroll web page.
cautions: Do not reproduce scrolling effects, hover states, or motion as decorative screenshot sequences in print.
The web version must not become a prerequisite for understanding the core case study.

strongest_reference.title: How to Write a Service-Planning Portfolio, with Sample PDF
strongest_reference.selection_reason: It supplies the clearest locally grounded combination of an actual Korean hiring sample, explicit project-count behavior, and a candid post-hire critique. The strongest transferable rule is to keep a master set of about five projects, tailor to roughly three when constrained, and make every selected project lead with role, result, and job relevance before process detail.

visual_patterns: Grid: Korean A4 resumes commonly use a narrow section-label rail and a wider content column, while case studies use a full-width project opener followed by structured evidence blocks.
Grid: compact developer portfolios favor a résumé-like continuous flow; design and planning portfolios allocate more space to one selected project's Problem, Solution, and Result sequence.
Typography: Korean sans-serif type, bold section labels, and strong numeric emphasis work better than decorative display typography for dense Hangul text.
Typography: body copy must be larger and shorter than many slide-derived samples; the local first-person critique explicitly warns that reviewers will skip small, dense text.
Color: white backgrounds, dark neutral text, and one company- or candidate-specific accent are common; accent color should organize links and headings rather than carry meaning alone.
Hierarchy: the first page typically combines name, target role, contact links, positioning statement, and a small set of core skills or proof points.
Hierarchy: project openers should surface title, period, role, work type, personal contribution, and one outcome before supporting detail.
Image treatment: enlarge one decisive screen, research artifact, or diagram and caption the inference; avoid grids of interfaces that become illegible on A4.
Tables: use compact metadata rows for role, team, duration, stack, and contribution, and small before-and-after tables for performance evidence.
Navigation: include a contents page only when the portfolio exceeds a short résumé format; always use running project titles and page numbers in multi-project PDFs.
content_patterns: Keep a master portfolio of roughly four to five credible projects, then submit about three highly relevant projects when a company imposes a page or presentation limit.
Order by confidence and relevance, not chronology; a Korean UX employer explicitly asks for the strongest project first.
Use the repeated case-study spine: problem or constraint, personal role, decision or method, implementation, evidence, and result.
State contribution boundaries clearly: what the candidate led, built, proposed, tested, documented, or supported.
For developer work, connect a technical intervention to an observed effect such as FCP, LCP, bundle size, interaction latency, user drop-off, or maintenance effort.
For product and design work, compress routine process and retain the research or experiment only when it changed the problem definition or design decision.
Show communication through collaboration context, feedback incorporated, documentation produced, and how a decision was explained to other functions.
Use plain Korean-language concepts in the source portfolio and minimize unexplained English or academic jargon; clarity carries more hiring value than sounding specialized.
Include one learning or failure narrative when it demonstrates a changed behavior, a better subsequent decision, or growth potential.
Treat repository, blog, live product, and prototype links as verification paths, while keeping the PDF's central argument self-contained.
a4_adaptation: Use A4 portrait pages with approximately 16–18 mm side margins and 16–20 mm top and bottom margins; do not shrink a 16:9 presentation or a wide continuous résumé onto A4.
Target a concise 6–10-page core document: cover/profile, one-page evidence summary, two to three selected projects at one to two pages each, and a compact closing/contact page.

Use Hozui SUIT typography tokens for reliable Korean composition, with display or heading tokens for project names, body-md for narrative, body-sm for metadata, and caption tokens only for short evidence notes.

Map the page to Hozui semantic colors: bg-canvas for paper, fg-default for text, fg-muted for metadata, stroke-default for rules, and a single accent token for links, project numbers, and evidence callouts.
Build a Hozui-style profile header with name, target role, one-sentence positioning, contact links, and no more than three proof points; keep the portrait optional.
Build a reusable project opener containing project number, title, period, team, role, contribution scope, one-sentence problem, and one headline outcome.
Use Hozui Chip or Badge patterns sparingly for role, platform, and a short stack; prevent long technology walls by moving secondary tools into a metadata line.
Create a repeated Challenge, Decision, Evidence, Outcome module using Hozui spacing, border, and semantic callout tokens; keep each module intact across page breaks.
Place before-and-after metrics in a compact table with metric name, baseline, result, measurement context, and source; do not rely on a large number without provenance.
Translate interactive web evidence into one annotated frame sequence or a QR/short link, ensuring the page remains understandable when links are unavailable.
Use print rules to prevent orphaned headings, split metric rows, detached captions, and clipped chips; embed SUIT fonts and keep text selectable.
Keep the PDF well below the employer's file-size ceiling by compressing screenshots appropriately and avoiding full-resolution decorative textures.
avoid_patterns: Do not copy the single-canvas wide résumé pattern literally; it forces tiny type and weak reading order on A4.
Avoid shrinking 16:9 slide decks onto portrait pages without rebuilding the grid and typography.
Avoid more than three equally detailed projects in the submitted core portfolio unless the employer explicitly requests broader coverage.
Avoid skill lists and technology logos that are not connected to a decision, implementation, or result.
Avoid team-level claims without a precise statement of personal contribution and collaboration boundaries.
Avoid unsupported percentages, speed improvements, or business outcomes without baseline, timeframe, measurement method, and attribution.
Avoid dense research chronology, every wireframe, or every implementation bullet; select the evidence that changed a decision.
Avoid English-heavy terminology and academic language when a plain explanation would be faster for a Korean recruiter or cross-functional reviewer.
Avoid low-contrast pastel textures, thin gray text, and small captions that degrade in grayscale printing.
Avoid making Notion toggles, web animation, GitHub, or a live product necessary to understand the project.
Avoid repeating a full self-introduction when a separate cover letter or career statement is part of the application package.
Avoid unstable filenames, archive-only delivery, and files near the maximum upload size.
fields.source_quality_notes: Research combined three first-party portfolio artifacts or samples, two Korean career-platform sources, one first-party employer requirement, and one Korean technology-media guide. Kim Daehyeon's PDF was verified as one 995-by-956-point page; Lee Hanbyeol's PDF was verified as six A4 pages; the service-planning sample linked by Rimppo was verified as a 10-page 16:9 PDF. The pxd notice directly states PDF format, a 50 MB ceiling, strongest-project-first ordering, and contribution disclosure. Wanted's 15-page developer report directly supplies survey percentages, while its Notion guide and the Yozm IT article provide editorial recommendations. Historical hiring rules and surveys are used as market signals, not assumed to be current requirements for every employer. Reported candidate metrics were not independently audited, so the adaptation recommends explicit provenance. Visual and A4 recommendations are analytical synthesis from the observed documents.
